result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.count_trails()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Count all trails (walks with distinct edges) from source to target. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L47180-L47321){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.count_trails( source, target, max_trails=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Count trails](/assets/graphs/count-trails.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed path A, B, C, D with a loop B, E, F back to B. Two trails reach D from A: the plain path in the accent color, and a teal one that goes around the loop and passes B twice without reusing an edge. The card lists both and the count, 2." width="100%"} A *trail* is a walk where all edges are distinct, but nodes may repeat. This is different from: - *path*: no repeated nodes or edges (most restrictive) - *trail*: no repeated edges, but nodes may repeat - *walk*: nodes and edges may repeat freely (least restrictive) Because a trail may loop through a node more than once, there are usually more trails than simple paths between two nodes. Counting them is useful when you care about how many distinct ways something can travel through a network without reusing a link, for example to gauge routing redundancy or to compare how "tangled" two parts of a network are. Each trail ends the first time it reaches `target=`; trails that pass through the target and come back to it later are not counted separately. On a directed graph edges are only followed in their own direction; on an undirected graph each edge can be crossed in either direction, but only once. Parallel edges count as distinct edges. Uses iterative depth-first search with edge tracking. The count can grow exponentially on dense graphs, so use the `max_trails=` parameter to limit computation. Use `enumerate_trails()` to get the trails themselves. The method does not modify the graph. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node the trails start from, given as an integer node ID or a string label. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node the trails end at, given as an integer node ID or a string label. If it is the same node as `source=`, the result is `1` (the trivial empty trail). [max_trails]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Upper bound on the counting work. If `None` (default), every trail is counted, however long that takes. Otherwise the search stops as soon as `max_trails=` trails have been found and the method returns `None`, so a numeric result is only returned when the true count is *less than* `max_trails=`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of distinct trails from source to target. Returns `None` if the count reached `max_trails=` (the true count is at least that large). Returns `1` if source and target are the same node. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If source or target node not found in graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A trail generalizes a path: it forbids reusing edges but allows revisiting nodes, which places it strictly between a walk (nothing forbidden) and a path (nothing repeated). Under the hood this is an iterative depth-first search with an explicit stack, tracking a visited-edge set that gets popped on backtrack. The count grows fast: between two nodes of a complete graph there are $2$ trails in $K_3$, $7$ in $K_4$, $58$ in $K_5$, and nearly $3{,}000$ in $K_6$, and moderately dense real graphs run into the millions. Setting `max_trails=` short-circuits the search once the cap is reached and returns `None`, which is essentially always the right choice on real-world graphs. The trivial case `source == target` counts as one (empty) trail. On undirected graphs, each edge can still be crossed in either direction, but only once. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a triangle `A -- B -- C -- A`, there are two distinct trails from `A` to `C`: the direct edge, and the longer route through `B`: ::: {#1836de50 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) graph.count_trails("A", "C") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Trails differ from simple paths when a route can loop back through a node. In this directed graph, the loop `B -> E -> F -> B` lets a trail pass through `B` twice, so there are two trails from `A` to `D` but only one simple path: ::: {#f9e246d4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("B", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "B"), # Loop back to B ] ) ) graph.count_trails("A", "D"), len(graph.get_all_simple_paths("A", "D")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (2, 1) ``` ::: ::: Real-world graphs can have an enormous number of trails, so `max_trails=` caps the search. A `None` result means the cap was hit -- here, at least 10,000 trails connect two members of the karate club network: ::: {#f2e5633e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} G = ec.karate_club() node_ids = list(G.get_node_ids()) G.count_trails(node_ids[0], node_ids[-1], max_trails=10000) is None ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: ::: On the small triangle from the first example the count (`2`) stays below a cap of `5`, so the exact number is returned, while a cap of `2` is reached and gives `None`: ::: {#722b752c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} triangle = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) triangle.count_trails("A", "C", max_trails=5), triangle.count_trails("A", "C", max_trails=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (2, None) ``` ::: :::
